item.title: Berakhot Part 2: Understanding the Structure and Meaning of a Blessing
item.description:
What does Baruch Atah Hashem actually mean? It is not man praising God, who has no needs, but a declaration that He is the source of all blessing. The shiur draws on the Rashba and the Maharal, explains why we say berakhot, and why they shift from You to He.

item.title: Berakhot Part 3: The Three Categories of Berakhot and Blessings in the Vernacular
item.description:
Every berakhah belongs to one of three categories. The shiur sets out blessings of benefit such as food and fragrance, blessings before a misvah, and blessings of praise, thanks and request like those of the Amidah, with examples such as seeing the sea or hearing thunder.

item.title: Berakhot Part 4: Saying Berakhot on Behalf of Others
item.description:
Can you say a berakhah on behalf of someone else? For misvot and blessings of praise you can, even if you have already done it yourself, but a blessing of benefit only if you are enjoying it too. The Shulhan Arukh says that if the other person can say it himself, he should.

item.title: Berakhot Part 5: Perhaps We Shouldn't Be Saying Berakhot on a Lot of the Food We Eat
item.description:
Should we say a berakhah on unhealthy food? The Gemara exempts harmful olive oil, and Rashi gives a different reason from other Rishonim. The shiur concludes that where harm is immediate, as with sugar for a diabetic, a berakhah is in vain, while ordinary unhealthy food is less clear.

item.title: Berakhot Part 6: Blessing on Soda Water
item.description:
When do we not say a berakhah on water? Only when drinking quenches thirst, so none for swallowing a pill, clearing the throat or drinking in advance to stay hydrated. Flavoured drinks always take a berakhah, and soda water depends on whether the person drinks it for the taste of the bubbles.

item.title: Berakhot Part 7: Berakhah on Papaya
item.description:
What is the berakhah on papaya, Ha-Es or Ha-Adamah? The Ben Ish Hai weighs the tree-versus-vegetable conditions, and the Radbaz on aubergine shows that a plant fruiting in its first year is not a tree. The conclusion is Ha-Adamah, the Sepharadi custom.

item.title: Berakhot Part 8: Blessing on Hydroponic Vegetables
item.description:
What berakhah do we say on hydroponic vegetables, grown in water and not in the ground? The Hazon Ish and Rav Ovadia Yoseph point to Shehakol, comparing mushrooms and the manna. Since ordinary vegetables are assumed to be ground-grown, Ha-Adamah stays unless you know it is hydroponic.

item.title: Berakhot Part 9: Berakhah on Fruit Pulp, Puree and Tropicana Orange Juice
item.description:
What berakhah goes on fruit pulp, puree and Tropicana orange juice? A mashed fruit keeps Ha-Es, a fully liquefied puree is disputed, and juice is Shehakol, even with bits in it. If you drink it mainly for the pulp, the berakhah is Ha-Es. Plain crisps are Ha-Adamah, but Pringles are Shehakol.

item.title: Berakhot Part 10: Berakhah on Popcorn
item.description:
What is the berakhah on popcorn? The Kaf HaHayim might say Shehakol since the corn has lost its form, but Rav Ovadia Yoseph and Rav Moshe Feinstein rule Ha-Adamah, because puffing is not grinding and everyone knows it is corn. Most poskim follow this.
